prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only 6 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use—so the measured senses cover distance only and miss the well-attested "racecourse" meaning noted by the lexica.

prose.def: An upright stake or post; in the NT, chiefly the Roman cross used to execute Jesus, and figuratively the self-denial and suffering of discipleship.
prose.article: σταυρός refers to an upright stake or pole, but in the New Testament it overwhelmingly means the Roman cross used for execution—rendered "cross" in 23 of its 28 occurrences (82%). It also appears in phrases about crucifying someone ("let cross," 2×), and Jesus uses it figuratively in the famous saying about taking up one's cross daily. A striking parallel comes from a 4th–5th century Christian prayer on papyrus that addresses "O God of the crosses that are laid upon us," treating crosses as the trials God both sends and eases. The lexica note that the earliest Greek writers used the word for a plain stake, with the crucifixion sense emerging only in later authors.

According to Swete, it specifically describes the ripe grape-cluster (as opposed to an unripe one) and emphasizes the grapes themselves rather than the woody cluster they grow on; the everyday papyri back this up, mentioning things like "a box of exceedingly good grapes."
prose.caution: The measured sense "thornbushes" reflects how one occurrence (Luke 6:44) was rendered in context, not a separate meaning of the word itself, which consistently denotes grapes.

prose.def: The roof of a building; used in idiomatic phrases like 'come under my roof' where it refers to the physical roof as the threshold of a home.
prose.article: Στέγη simply means the roof of a building, and that is how it is rendered in all three of its New Testament appearances. In two passages (Matthew 8:8, Luke 7:6) it is part of the phrase "to come under my roof," where the roof stands for the whole home—the centurion saying he is unworthy to host Jesus. Everyday Koine papyri use the word the same way, including a tax-dodging case where owners had "taken down the upper story" (στέγας) of a building to avoid having officials lodged there.
prose.caution: With only three New Testament occurrences and two in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, though every source agrees on the basic meaning.

prose.def: To bear up under or endure patiently, possibly with a nuance of covering over; the sense 'conceal' is also attested, especially at 1 Corinthians 13:7.
senseLabels: bears/covers all things (1CO 13:7, disputed: endure or conceal)
prose.article: In the New Testament στέγω means to bear up under hardship and keep enduring, and that is how the Majority Standard Bible renders all four occurrences—"bear" twice and "bears things" once, with one instance absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word's root idea is to cover or roof over, and from that came two branches: covering to conceal, or covering to ward off and endure; Abbott-Smith notes the "keep secret" sense is possible at 1 Corinthians 13:7 ("love covers all things"), though the MSB and BSB read it as enduring. A nice everyday parallel appears in an Oxyrhynchus papyrus where a writer says his father did him much harm "and I endured (ἔστεξα) until you came."
prose.caution: With only four occurrences and the "conceal" versus "endure" senses overlapping, the rendering of 1 Corinthians 13:7 is genuinely debated.

prose.def: Describing a woman as barren or unable to bear children; used literally of individuals (Luke) and figuratively in typological quotation (Galatians).
prose.article: This word describes a woman who cannot have children, and every New Testament use refers to exactly that—it appears 4 times in the Byzantine text, always of barren women (Luke 1:7, 1:36, 23:29, Galatians 4:27). In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times across 8 books, almost always translating the Hebrew word ʿaqar (12 of 14 times), the standard term for childlessness. The form is striking for its staying power: Moulton-Milligan notes that steíra survives unchanged in Modern Greek, and the word appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well.
prose.caution: The three labels listed by the renderings all reflect the single sense "barren"; differences are just sentence context, not distinct meanings.

prose.def: In the middle voice, to restrain or withdraw oneself from something or someone, whether avoiding criticism or keeping away from disorderly persons.
senseLabels: to withdraw or hold oneself back (middle voice): avoid blame or keep away from persons
prose.article: In the Byzantine New Testament στέλλω appears only twice, both times in the middle voice meaning to restrain oneself, withdraw, or steer clear of something—as in avoiding any criticism (2 Corinthians 8:20) and keeping away from disorderly believers (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The word's root sense is to set, place, or arrange, and the everyday papyri show it commonly meaning to send (for instance, P Oxy 1843 mentions linen garments "sent me"). Notably, the seafaring world used it of furling or shortening sails (Homer), and from that image of drawing things in came the New Testament sense of pulling oneself back.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 New Testament occurrences (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), so the range here rests on a very small sample.

prose.def: A wreath or garland, in its one NT occurrence used to adorn sacrificial animals in a pagan religious ceremony.
senseLabels: a wreath or garland (used in sacrificial or ceremonial contexts)
prose.article: Στέμμα refers to a wreath or garland, formed from a root meaning to wrap or encircle. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 14:13), it names the garlands the priest of Zeus brought to adorn the sacrificial animals when the crowd at Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas. Everyday papyri broaden the picture: the word shows up in connection with guilds and even names an official "in charge of the stemmata," showing it was common administrative vocabulary in Koine Egypt.

prose.def: A deep groan or sigh expressing pain, distress, or longing.
prose.article: στεναγμός refers to a heartfelt groan or sigh, the kind that escapes someone in pain or deep longing. Although classical sources often distinguish στέφανος (a victor's wreath) from διάδημα (a royal crown), Moulton-Milligan warns this distinction shouldn't be pressed too hard, since στέφανος is not infrequently used for a king's crown too. prose.def: To stand or remain in place; often used figuratively in direct exhortations meaning to hold one's position or persevere in faith.
prose.article: στήκω means simply "to stand," but in the New Testament it leans heavily toward the figurative sense of standing firm or holding your ground—4 of its 8 Byzantine occurrences are rendered "stand firm," the other 3 as plain "stand." It's actually a newer Koine verb formed from the perfect tense of ἵστημι ("to stand"), and it survives into Modern Greek as στέκω. A striking detail from the papyri: in one inscription it's used interchangeably with another late form for "stand," suggesting the supposed emphatic force of the word shouldn't be pushed too hard.
prose.caution: Moulton-Milligan warns that the emphatic "firmness" sometimes read into this verb may be overstated, since late Greek freely coined such forms.

A vivid older sense survives in Luke 9:51, where Jesus "set his face" toward Jerusalem, echoing a Hebrew idiom; the everyday Koine papyri likewise show it used quite literally, as in propping something against a beam.

prose.def: A mark, brand, or scar pricked or burned into the skin, often signaling ownership or service.
prose.article: Στίγμα comes from a root meaning "to prick," and it refers to a mark made by puncturing or branding the skin — the kind used to show who owned a person or animal. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:17, where Paul speaks of carrying "the marks of Jesus" on his body; commentators generally take these as the scars he gathered through his apostolic suffering. The word also turns up once in the Septuagint, at Song of Songs 1:11, translating a Hebrew word for ornamental points or studs, and Moulton-Milligan notes it was a familiar term in everyday Koine documents.

prose.def: An army, especially one camped or on the move, viewed as an organized military force.
prose.article: στρατόπεδον combines the words for "army" and "plain," and its root meaning is a military camp—the ground where troops pitch their tents. By extension it came to mean the body of troops itself, and that is how it works in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 21:20), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "armies" in all instances. Notably, the everyday papyri preserve both senses: an inscription from A.D. 216 calls Julia Domna "mother of the unconquered armies," while a document from 128 B.C. uses it for an actual royal camp.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence even though wider Koine evidence is solid.

prose.def: To turn or pivot (usually oneself) to face a new direction, or figuratively to change course, be converted, or transform something entirely.
prose.article: στρέφω is the everyday verb for turning—most often someone pivoting their body to face a different way, as when Jesus "turned" to address his disciples. The two measured senses are really one idea in different grammatical dress: the participle "turned" (9×, 47%) and the plain "turn" (7×, 37%), with the Berean Standard Bible matching independently 100% and 86% of the time. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew הָפַך ("overturn, change") most often, 13 of 36 times, and a charming everyday papyrus describes a constellation "that turns the axis"—the same word used of the sky's rotation.
prose.caution: Lexicons list a figurative "change" or "convert" sense (Matt 18:3; Rev 11:6), but this shows up only in rare renderings, so the metaphorical range is real yet thinly attested in the measured data.

prose.def: Forceful, wanton luxury — the vigorous, self-indulgent excess and insolence of someone reveling in extravagant wealth.
prose.article: στρῆνος describes over-the-top luxury and the insolence that comes with it — living lavishly and wantonly. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 18:3, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it as drunk, wealthy extravagance. It's a late, fairly rare word (first attested in a Greek comic poet around 300 B.C.), and its single Septuagint use in 2 Kings 19:28 is striking: there it renders a Hebrew word and is applied to the Assyrian king's arrogance reaching God's ears.

prose.def: A small bird, the sparrow, used in Jesus's teaching to illustrate God's care for even the cheapest and most common creatures.
prose.article: Στρουθίον is the everyday word for a sparrow, technically a diminutive of στρουθός (a larger bird). The two "measured senses" here are really the same bird in slightly different phrasings—half its New Testament uses come in the expression "worth more than sparrows," stressing how cheap these birds were. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew צִפּוֹר (bird), and a Greek food-account papyrus prices a large στρουθός at 8 drachmae, which the editors think may actually refer to an ostrich.
prose.caution: The word's range is unusually wide—from a tiny sparrow to possibly an ostrich in the papyri—so the parent term στρουθός could mean a much larger bird than the New Testament sense suggests.

prose.def: To sit together with others, whether informally among bystanders or formally as part of an official assembly, using either dative or μετά + genitive constructions.

prose.article: Built from σύν ("with") and κάθημαι ("to sit"), this verb simply means to sit alongside others, whether warming yourself by a fire among bystanders or taking a seat as part of a group. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "sat warmed by" once (Mark 14:54), with the other occurrence absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The papyri show the same plain Koine use: in a case before the Emperor Claudius, senators "sit along with" the Emperor as advisors, and a record even notes clerks sitting up through the night by lamplight.

prose.def: A coincidence or chance happening, used in the phrase "by chance" for something that occurs without prior planning.
prose.article: συγκυρία means a coincidence or chance occurrence, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 10:31, in the phrase κατὰ συγκυρίαν ("by chance")—describing how a priest happened to come down the same road in the parable of the Good Samaritan. The word turns up more often in later Greek writers and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where the related verb συγκυρέω was commonly used for the "appurtenances" belonging to a house. Symmachus used it once in the Septuagint at 1 Kings 6:9, matching the Hebrew word for "chance" or "happening."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse plus comparative evidence from papyri and late writers.

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence of συγκυρία appears here in the phrase κατὰ συγκυρίαν, directly confirming the definition's core claim that the word means a chance or unplanned happening.
Strong's gloss 'concurrence, i.e. accident' and Dodson's 'coincidence, accident, chance' corroborate the definition's rendering 'by chance' for something occurring without prior planning.

Abbott-Smith's citation of Hippocrates and Ecclesiastes alongside the Symmachus LXX reference at 1 Kings 6:9 confirms that the word's meaning of 'chance/coincidence' is consistent across its full comparative attestation.

prose.def: To rejoice together with someone or to take pleasure in something; sometimes carrying the sense of congratulating another person in their joy.
senseLabels: to be glad alongside; to congratulate
prose.article: This verb combines "with" (σύν) and "rejoice" (χαίρω) to mean sharing gladness alongside another person. Of its 7 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "rejoice" 4 times (67%), with single instances of "love takes pleasure" and "glad." Everyday Koine papyri show the same warmth: a mother writes to her son that she "rejoiced for you and for myself" upon learning he was studying Egyptian script. The classical lexica add a secondary sense, "to congratulate," which Abbott-Smith notes for Philippians.
prose.caution: Evidence is moderate with only 7 occurrences, and lexicons add a "congratulate" sense not separately reflected in the measured renderings.

prose.def: To throw people into confusion, uproar, or bewilderment; used of agitated crowds and confounded minds, always in Acts.
prose.article: συγχέω literally means to pour things together, and from there it came to mean stirring people up into confusion or commotion. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, all in Acts, where translators render it differently each time—from a crowd in turmoil to a mind left bewildered—so no single English word captures it. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri: one writer (P Oxy XVI.1873) says "I feel my reasoning faculties confused," showing the same sense of mental bewilderment. In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words, most often בָּלַל ("to mingle") and רָגַז ("to be agitated").
prose.caution: With only 5 occurrences, each translated by a different English word, the word's force depends heavily on context rather than a fixed meaning.

prose.def: To have dealings or use something jointly with others; in the New Testament, to associate with someone across a social or ethnic boundary.
senseLabels: have dealings with / associate with someone
prose.article: This verb literally means "to use jointly with," and in the New Testament it describes having social dealings or associating with people. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 4:9, where it explains that Jews do not associate with Samaritans. The everyday Koine papyri show its more concrete side: one document from the third century B.C. uses it of jointly using forty donkeys in preparations for an official's visit, so the word ranges from sharing physical resources to sharing human company.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

issues: The syntactic role data tags the single occurrence as 'vocative,' which is almost certainly a mis-tag for the finite verb form in JOH 4:9; the definition should not mask this data anomaly, but more importantly the article does not address it.

The definition phrase 'associate together with others' is slightly redundant and imprecise; the classical and papyri evidence shows the primary meaning is 'use jointly/in common,' with social association as a derived (metaphorical) sense — the definition presents only the derived sense.

The KJV gloss 'have dealings with' and Dodson's 'I have dealings with' capture the JOH 4:9 context more precisely than 'associate together,' which sounds more voluntary and social than the ethnic-boundary sense the verse conveys.

The supporting article mentions the papyri evidence of sharing physical resources but the definition itself does not flag this literal dimension, leaving readers with only the social/metaphorical sense.

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence uses the word to explain that Jews do not 'have dealings with' (οὐ συγχρῶνται) Samaritans, confirming the social-contact sense but in the specific context of ethnic-communal boundary avoidance, not mere voluntary association.

The same verse is the only receipt available given the hapax status of this word in the NT; the definition's 'associate together with others' softens the boundary-marking force the word carries in this ethnic-relations context, showing where revision is needed.

prose.def: A state of confusion or riotous disorder, especially the tumult of an agitated crowd (the corpus sense label 'Soon' is a data error; all lexical sources consistently render this word as 'confusion').
prose.article: σύγχυσις describes confusion or disorder, and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 19:29) it refers to the uproar of an agitated crowd. Built on the verb συγχέω (to pour together, mix up), it carries the idea of things thrown into chaotic disorder. In the Septuagint it appears four times, including Genesis 11:9, where it stands behind the name Babel; elsewhere it translates the Hebrew word for tumult or panic. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one inscription even speaks of someone as the "instigator of the whole confusion."
prose.caution: The Majority Standard Bible's rendering "Soon" in the measured data does not match the lexical sources, which consistently define the word as "confusion" or "disturbance"; treat the listed sense label with caution given only one New Testament occurrence.

prose.def: To live together with someone, either in mutual human solidarity or in shared life with Christ, present and future.
senseLabels: live together with (Christ or another person)
prose.article: συζάω combines "with" (σύν) and "live" (ζάω) to mean sharing life in common with another person. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "live" in two of those, while the third is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Abbott-Smith notes it stands opposite "to die together with" in 2 Corinthians 7:3 and elsewhere describes life in union with Christ; a charming touch from the papyri is a second-century BC epigram on the playwright Menander, praising one who "lived along with" him.
prose.caution: This is a rare word with only 3 occurrences, so its full range rests on thin evidence.

issues: The syntactic role data shows 2 occurrences as vocative, which is unusual for a verb and likely reflects a parsing artifact or error in Macula data, but the definition does not acknowledge any morphological complexity

The definition emphasizes 'sharing the same life and existence' as a general concept, but Abbott-Smith clarifies it specifically refers to life in union with Christ in Romans 6:8 and 2 Timothy 2:11, with 2 Corinthians 7:3 being the only interpersonal (non-Christological) use — the definition blurs this distinction

The phrase 'whether now or beyond death' is partially supported (2TI 2:11 implies future life, ROM 6:8 implies present and future life with Christ) but is an addition not clearly warranted by 2CO 7:3, where Paul speaks of mutual human life and death with the Corinthians — the definition risks over-theologizing the 2CO 7:3 usage
The definition does not capture Strong's nuance of 'co-survive,' which is relevant to the eschatological sense in 2TI 2:11

receipts.how: Paul's use of συζάω with Christ as the implied co-subject demonstrates the primary Christological sense: believers who died with Christ will also live with him, supporting the 'life in union with Christ' reading.

Paul tells the Corinthians 'you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together,' showing the word used for mutual interpersonal solidarity rather than the Christological sense — the definition's universal phrasing fits here but obscures the contrast with the other two uses.

The faithful saying 'if we died with him, we will also live with him' shows the eschatological co-survival sense that Strong's highlights, partially supporting 'beyond death' but tied specifically to Christ.

audit.author_note: Paul uses συζάω in two distinct registers: in 2 Corinthians 7:3 for mutual human solidarity, and in Romans 6:8 and 2 Timothy 2:11 (the Pastorals) for eschatological life in union with Christ — readers of 2 Corinthians may be misled by a definition that foregrounds the Christological sense.
